p: Website accessibility means building a site that people can use whatever their abilities, devices or circumstances. That includes people who are blind or have low vision, people who are deaf or hard of hearing, people with motor difficulties who cannot use a mouse, and people with cognitive differences. It also includes someone squinting at a phone in bright sunlight or holding a baby in one arm.

For a business owner, accessibility is partly about doing the right thing and partly about practical self-interest: more people can buy from you, your site is easier for everyone, and many accessibility improvements also help search engines. This guide explains the basics in plain English, with the most valuable fixes first, free tools to check your own site and a checklist you can hand to a developer.

h: Why accessibility matters for a business
p: A large share of any customer base has some kind of disability or temporary limitation. If your booking form cannot be completed with a keyboard, or your text is too faint to read, those people will leave and often will not tell you why.

There is also overlap with other good practice. Descriptive headings, clear link text, text alternatives for images and fast, stable pages help screen reader users, but they also help search engines understand your content and help everyone skim a page. Accessible sites tend to be cleaner and easier to maintain.

Finally, there is the legal side. Whether accessibility is a legal requirement depends on your country, your sector and the size of your organisation, and the rules differ widely. Many laws and public-sector policies point to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) as the standard. If you are unsure whether rules apply to you, ask a qualified adviser in your area rather than guessing.

h: WCAG in plain English: the four principles
p: WCAG is published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). Its guidelines are organised around four principles, often remembered by the word POUR. Content must be perceivable, meaning users can see or hear it in some form. It must be operable, meaning users can navigate and use controls with different input methods. It must be understandable, meaning the text and behaviour are clear and predictable. And it must be robust, meaning it works with a range of browsers and assistive technologies.

Each guideline has success criteria at three levels: A, AA and AAA. Most laws and policies that reference WCAG aim for level AA, so that is a sensible target for a business website. You do not need to memorise criteria numbers. Focus on the practical habits below.
If you do only a handful of things, do these. They address the problems that block people most often.
list: Text alternatives: every meaningful image needs short, descriptive alt text. Purely decorative images should have empty alt text so screen readers skip them.

Colour contrast: body text needs enough contrast against its background. WCAG AA asks for a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. Light grey text on white is the classic failure.
Keyboard access: everything that works with a mouse must work with the Tab, Enter, Space and arrow keys, and users must always be able to see where the keyboard focus is.
Form labels: every field needs a visible label connected to it. A placeholder is not a label because it disappears as soon as someone starts typing.
Headings and structure: use real heading levels in order, so that screen reader users can jump through the page the way sighted users skim it.
Link text: avoid links that say only click here or read more. The link text should make sense out of context.
Captions and transcripts: provide captions for videos and transcripts for audio so that deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and people watching without sound, get the same information.

p: WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023. It builds on earlier versions rather than replacing them, so a site that follows 2.1 is most of the way there. It added several success criteria that matter on modern sites, including Focus Not Obscured (keyboard focus must not be hidden behind sticky headers or cookie banners), Dragging Movements (anything that needs dragging must also work with a simple click or tap), and Target Size (Minimum), which asks for interactive targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels in most cases.

It also added Consistent Help, which asks that help options such as a contact link appear in the same place across pages, Redundant Entry, which avoids making users type the same information twice in a process, and Accessible Authentication, which avoids forcing users to solve memory or puzzle tests to log in. The old criterion 4.1.1 on parsing was removed as obsolete. For a small business, the practical message is to avoid cramped tap targets, hidden focus and unnecessarily difficult sign-in or checkout steps.

h: How to test your own site for free
p: You do not need an expensive audit to find the biggest problems. Start with automated tools, then add two quick manual checks, because automated tools only detect a portion of accessibility issues.
list: Run Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools and read the accessibility section for flagged contrast, label and alt text problems.
Use a browser extension such as axe DevTools or WAVE to highlight issues directly on the page.

Do the keyboard test: put your mouse aside and try to complete the main task on your site, such as sending a contact form, using only the Tab and Enter keys. Note anywhere you get stuck or lose track of focus.
Try a screen reader briefly: VoiceOver is built into Apple devices, and NVDA is a free option for Windows. Even five minutes will show you how your page sounds.
Zoom the page to 200 percent and check that text still fits and nothing overlaps.

h: A worked example: a restaurant website
p: Consider a fictional restaurant site with a photo-heavy home page, a PDF menu and a table-reservation form. A quick audit would likely find the following. The hero photo and dish images have no alt text. The menu is a scanned PDF that a screen reader cannot read. The reservation form uses placeholders instead of labels, and the date picker cannot be used with a keyboard. The pale grey opening-hours text fails contrast, and a sticky banner covers the focused field as people tab down the form.

The fixes are all modest. Add alt text to meaningful images, publish the menu as real text on a page, add visible labels, switch to an accessible date field, darken the grey text and make sure the sticky element does not cover focused controls. None of this changes the look of the site much, but together it turns a form that excludes some customers into one that works for everyone, including people booking one-handed on a phone.

list: Relying on an accessibility overlay or plugin that promises instant compliance. These widgets cannot fix underlying markup problems and can create new ones; fix the source code instead.
Using colour alone to convey meaning, such as red text for errors with no icon or message, which fails for colour-blind users.
Removing the focus outline for visual neatness without providing a clear replacement.
Hiding essential information inside images of text or inaccessible PDFs.
Testing only once. Every new page, banner and plugin can introduce new problems, so build checks into your routine.
Run Lighthouse and axe or WAVE on your home page, contact page and checkout or booking page.
Fix contrast problems and add alt text to meaningful images.
Add visible labels to every form field and clear error messages.
Complete your main task using only the keyboard, and fix any traps or invisible focus.
Check heading order and make link text descriptive.
Add captions to videos and replace image-only content with real text.
Ensure tap targets are large enough and sticky elements do not cover focus.
Publish a short accessibility statement with a contact route for feedback.

p: Is accessibility the same as SEO? No, but they overlap. Clear headings, descriptive links, alt text and well-structured content help both. Accessibility, however, goes further, covering things like keyboard use and contrast that search engines do not directly reward.

Do I need to meet WCAG level AAA? Usually not. Level AA is the common target in laws and policies, and AAA is not recommended as a blanket requirement because some of its criteria cannot be met for all content.
Will accessibility make my site ugly? No. Good accessibility is mostly about structure, contrast and clear interaction. Many of the most admired sites are also very accessible.
How often should I check? Check after any significant change, and run a quick automated scan monthly. Treat it like proofreading: small, regular checks beat one big audit every few years.

list: Accessible websites work for more people and are often cleaner and better for search too.
Aim for WCAG 2.2 level AA as a practical target, and check your local legal requirements separately.
Fix alt text, contrast, labels, keyboard access, headings and link text first.
Use free tools such as Lighthouse, axe and WAVE, and always add a manual keyboard test.
Avoid quick-fix overlays and make accessibility part of your regular site maintenance.
